subject: maths
title: Expressions — expand, factorise and simplify

slides.heading: Expressions — the building blocks of algebra
slides.body: An algebraic expression combines numbers and letters using operations, but has no equals sign. Expanding removes brackets by multiplying out; factorising reverses this by taking out a common factor; simplifying collects like terms into the shortest form. These three skills sit underneath almost every algebra topic — equations, quadratics, and rearranging formulae all rely on them.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: Expanding and factorising rules
slides.formula: a(b + c) = ab + ac | (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd | Factorising: find the HCF of all terms and take it outside the bracket
slides.formulaExplained: For a single bracket, multiply the term outside by every term inside: a(b + c) = ab + ac. For double brackets, multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second — four multiplications in total. Factorising is the reverse: find the largest factor every term shares (the HCF), write it outside a bracket, and divide each term by it to fill the inside.
slides.whenToUse: Expanding: whenever an expression contains brackets that need to be removed before simplifying or solving. Factorising: whenever you need to reverse an expanded expression or simplify a fraction involving algebra.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: Expand and simplify (x + 3)(x − 4).

steps.instruction: Multiply the first term in the first bracket (x) by each term in the second bracket.
Multiply the second term in the first bracket (+3) by each term in the second bracket.
Collect all four terms and simplify like terms.
Check by factorising the result back — two numbers that multiply to −12 and add to −1 are −4 and +3.
steps.working: (x − 4)(x + 3) — the original brackets in the other order. ✓

slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Expanding a double bracket with only two multiplications instead of four — e.g. writing (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − 12, missing the −4x and +3x cross-terms entirely.
mistakes.correction: Every term in the first bracket must multiply every term in the second: four products total. Use a grid to keep track: x×x, x×(−4), 3×x, 3×(−4).

mistakes.mistake: Sign error when multiplying two negatives — e.g. expanding (x − 5)(x − 3) and writing −5 × −3 = −15 instead of +15, giving x² − 8x − 15 instead of x² − 8x + 15.
mistakes.correction: Negative × negative = positive. When both terms are negative, the constant at the end is always positive: (x − 5)(x − 3) = x² − 8x + 15.

mistakes.mistake: Expanding a single bracket by only multiplying the first term — e.g. writing 4(3x − 2) = 12x − 2 instead of 12x − 8.
mistakes.correction: The factor outside multiplies every term inside the bracket without exception: 4(3x − 2) = 4 × 3x + 4 × (−2) = 12x − 8.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: Single bracket: a(b + c) = ab + ac — multiply every term inside by the term outside.
keyFacts.examTip: There are no exceptions — every term inside the bracket gets multiplied, including constants with signs.

keyFacts.fact: Double brackets: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd — four multiplications, every term in the first bracket with every term in the second.
keyFacts.examTip: Use a 2×2 grid to avoid missing a product: x and +3 across the top, x and −4 down the side.

keyFacts.fact: To factorise, find the HCF of all terms and write it outside the bracket: 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3).
keyFacts.examTip: Check by re-expanding: 3x(2x + 3) = 6x² + 9x. If you get back to the start, the factorisation is correct.

keyFacts.fact: Like terms share the same letter(s) raised to the same power. Only like terms can be collected: 3x² + 5x² = 8x², but 3x² + 5x cannot be simplified further.
keyFacts.examTip: 3x and 3x² are NOT like terms — the power of x is different. Do not add them.
